utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, there is a difficulty, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder, Your Honour, if we might go into private session while I indicate the nature of the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are two reasons for reassembling. First, regrettably I overlooked the matter that we had moved in private session when we made adjournment decisions and announced them and that needs to be on the public record. But secondly we have now received a brief medical report, and it seems --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes could I just indicate if it could again be in private session for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're in public session. What is the reason for the private session, Mr. Mansfield?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Because it concerns confidential matters of -- which you have on that report. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Frankly, the Chamber sees no matter of confidence to justify private in this sort of issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, certainly Mr. Limaj indicated this morning through others, not to me personally but through others who were coming to Court, two things about today and one of them was anxious that these matters were not discussed in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that may be an anxiety of his personally but in terms of justification for this being a private session, the Chamber doesn't accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can't take it further, but that was the express wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, are you in a position yet any instructions about at least the evidence in chief continuing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm afraid not directly, only indirectly. The indirect indication that was given early this morning to others was that there was a sincere wish that matters did not proceed in his absence whether in chief or in cross-examination. I make it perfectly clear that I haven't been able to speak to him to confirm that that, but that was the information that was received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber has received a brief medical report indicating that because of an a temporary health infection of the throat, Mr. Limaj is unable to attend Court today and it appears tomorrow, and his position will be re-evaluated on Monday. We must, therefore, adjourn today, given the circumstance that his counsel has not been able to obtain instructions. We would propose to ask, Mr. Mansfield, that you do what you can to see whether instructions can be obtained to facilitate a sitting tomorrow. The sitting would go, I believe in fairness to your client, no further than evidence in chief, so that he should be present through cross-examination. If that doesn't occur, there seems a considerable likelihood, even if we're able to continue on Monday, that the present witness would not finish in the time listed next week, and that would be inconvenient and undesirable for many reasons and would put us even further behind in our own sitting timetable. As you realise we have been losing time steadily in this trial and are now over a fortnight behind schedule. So we would encourage you to seek as well you may instructions about the trial continuing tomorrow in the absence of your client. And with that in mind, we would propose to adjourn now until tomorrow morning at 9.00, and we would hope that by then, it will be possible to continue. I don't think any comment is called for unless you see a particular problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I just wanted to rise not to deal with, of course, Mr. Mansfield or Mr. Limaj's obvious difficulties, but a comment that Your Honours just made which is regarding the question of losing time steadily and a fortnight behind schedule. I venture to suggest that is a pessimistic view that is not shared by the bar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This sound encouraging, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I mean it to be. Your Honours won't know that on the 3rd of March all parties met in this building for a review of the case, as it were, what has happened and more importantly what is to come. And an important of that meeting, and I'm looking at my own contemporary rather note of it, dealt with evidence to be called. And it is clear from that meeting and all subsequent discussions that the aim of the bar to conclude the Prosecution case around the middle of April remains the view. Now, give or take a day or two, a few days, perhaps even a week, maybe even two. But, Your Honours that is certainly the position the bar understands the case to be in, notwithstanding as a former of prime minister of us "this little local difficulty" of today. Whether the Chamber has other information that we don't have that gave rise to Your Honours' view that time was slipping by, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My understanding was early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I think we're going to do better than that. I think we're go to do better than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Maybe the time we're losing today can be spent in discussions between counsel to see where they feel themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Some of it already has. I can tell Your Honour that, certainly between myself and Mr. Whiting. And we are ad idem as to the intention to finish in and around the area -- their case, at around the time I have been indicating to you. Your Honour, I only rose to mention all this in case it should be in any way imposing itself upon the view that the Court may take of the present predicament that we are in. Your Honour, I can say that all experts on -- but one are agreed, and we're pretty much in agreement about him. We have saved weeks of evidence on experts in this case. I mean literally weeks. We're go to hear Mr. Coo and he is going to be much shorter, I predict, than we ever would have thought. And all other experts we are not troubling to you hear orally. But one. Oh yes. And it's they who are troubling you, because they insist upon calling Mr. Maart we don't want to. So, Your Honour, I simply add all that into the equation. That's got Mr. Whiting to his feet. I simply add all that so the Court is aware of where we think we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have very grateful for your observations, Mr. Topolski, and encouraged and even heartened by what you say. But Mr. Whiting is going to put cream on the cake or dampen the whole thing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, my sense is we are -- continually evaluating which witnesses should be called and whether we can drop witnesses. But my sense at the present is that our goal of mid-April has probably already slipped by one week because of prior delays and I think even now, looking ahead with this current difficulty, even thinking optimistically, I think that is going to cause another week. So I think that does bring us, probably until the end of April. However, we are trying to shorten things as much as possible and try to reach agreement and try to drop any witnesses that we can drop. And we will continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. The Chamber is very grateful for the efforts made by all counsel, we or they, to ensure that that trial can proceed as efficiently as is consistent with the interest of the parties. And we're very encouraged to hear that there may even at this stage a prospect of finishing before the beginning of May. All that aside, it remains the case that there are obvious practical and personal reasons why it would be in everyone's interest if the present witness could conclude his evidence before the considerable break at the end of next week. And for that reason, if it is possible to sit tomorrow, it would, I think, give us just the extra time that can ensure that that objective is achieved. But we will have to wait and see whether that becomes practical or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just address you on that matter, because so far today, beyond the doctor, no one else has been able to see him. I think the practicality of attempting to get a satisfactory answer from him with reference to the medical report is -- is low. And therefore, the suggestion I have -- and it won't, I think we all agree, jeopardise this timetable is that in fact if he were allowed to recuperate for two days -- that is, today and tomorrow -- that he could then be here in person on Monday. If he couldn't be here on Monday, then obviously at that stage I had already indicated to others that one possible recourse is that he is either able to see on a monitor in the unit what is happening here, or at least is provided with a transcript which would -- in Albanian, which would ease matters because I think he would recognise the need to finish this witness before the Easter break. Were it to take that course on Monday, as opposed to earlier, then this witness would still be finished because the estimate is I think from Mr. Whiting that he may have best part of another session to go still, but perhaps not all of it. And I have already indicated, and my estimates in the past have been reasonably accurate, that I would be about four hours which is less than one session, just. And Mr. Topolski perhaps less than that. So that we would still finish before the Easter break because I understand Mr. Guy-Smith may have very little. Therefore, I think on that basis, it wouldn't -- it wouldn't therefore harm the timetable. I'm just trying to be realistic about it, so whether waiting another day for a situation where I'm probably not going to be able to see him today. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In view of those encouraging estimates we hadn't wanted to press about how long cross-examination would take in view of the importance of the witness. But in view of those encouraging estimates the practicality of what you propose commends itself. So that being the case, Mr. Mansfield, we would adjourn until Monday and hope that by then either your client is well enough to be with us or that on Monday morning alternative arrangements can be put in place that will assist him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will therefore adjourn and resume sitting on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of March, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.03 a.m.,
